items.title: Bookkeeping for a small business
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Bookkeeping is recording every sale and every cost as it happens, so you can always say what the business earned and spent. Keep business money in its own bank account, keep every receipt and invoice, and record each transaction against a category such as sales, materials or rent. Once a month, reconcile: match your records to the bank statement and explain any difference. Under accruals accounting a sale is recorded when it is earned or invoiced, and a cost when it is incurred, even if cash moves later; under cash accounting it is recorded when money moves. Records must be kept for the period tax law requires, which in the UK is generally at least five to six years. Good books make tax, loans and selling the business far easier.

items.title: Ongoing tax and VAT
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Running a business means putting tax aside as you earn, not when the bill arrives. Set aside a fixed share of every payment in a separate account. Know which taxes apply: income tax or corporation tax on profit, VAT if you are registered (in the UK you must register once taxable sales pass the registration threshold, and may register earlier), and payroll taxes if you employ people. Each has deadlines and late penalties. VAT is collected for the tax authority: you charge it on sales, reclaim it on business purchases, and pay or reclaim the difference. Keep records that show how each figure was reached, and ask an accountant to confirm what applies to you.

items.title: Warning signs of trouble
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Most failing businesses show warning signs months before the end: cash that is lower every month, suppliers and tax paid late, one debt used to pay another, an overdraft always at its limit, customers who pay slower, a falling order book, and staff leaving. Watch a short list of figures every week: cash in the bank, money owed to you, and money you owe with its due dates. The earlier you act, the more options you have: talk to creditors, cut costs, raise money or restructure. Directors of a limited company have legal duties to creditors when insolvency is likely, so take advice from a licensed insolvency practitioner or accountant early, not at the last moment.

items.title: Paying creditors when a business closes
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: When a business closes, it must deal with what it owes before owners take anything. If it can pay all its debts (it is solvent), it pays creditors in full, and any money left can be shared among the owners. If it cannot pay everyone (it is insolvent), the law sets an order: the costs of the process first, then secured creditors, then certain preferential creditors (such as some employee claims), then unsecured creditors who share what is left in proportion, and owners last. Paying one creditor ahead of others in an insolvency can be challenged. An insolvent closure needs a licensed insolvency practitioner, so this is a point to take advice, not to guess.
